name: Najma Omary
feedback: Strong, honest submission. Your standout is Task 7: you decoded all three segments, correctly named the empty-signature alg:none acceptance (not "weak crypto") as the precise root cause, cited RFC 7519 6.1 plus CVE-2015-9235, and gave the correct two-part fix of an explicit allow-list plus server-side authorization on the verified sub rather than the role claim. You also handled both honesty traps with integrity, on Artefact A you said the Vigenere plaintext could not be fully recovered rather than inventing one, and on D2 artefact 04 you said it could not be cracked from rockyou or wordlists instead of faking a secret, which is exactly the discipline we test for and earned you no penalty. Your biggest weakness is D2 artefact 04 itself, you stopped at "couldn't crack" but the full answer was to recover the hard-coded secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 from the leaked /legacy-admin/login.php source, then prove the captured token's HS256 signature does not verify because it was tampered, then forge a valid amaka.eze token, the lesson being that a tampered token is not a wordlist problem at all, the secret lives in the source. To improve D1, keep the table but add the exact section number to each standard column, for example RFC 7519 7.2 for the exp and alg claims and RFC 7518 3.1 for the JOSE alg values, since a standard without a section number only earns half credit. On Task 10 Q1, lead with a board-ready headline such as "the algorithm is not the asset, the key is" so the CFO hears the one-line risk, and on Q3 name exactly one audit pattern, you blended unverified token claims with plaintext secrets in config, so pick one such as "audit every config and backup file for plaintext keys and secrets" and evidence it. Minor Task 6 fix, bcrypt is CPU-hard via its cost factor, not memory-hard, only Argon2id and scrypt are memory-hard, so correct that framing. Tighten these rows and citation section numbers and this is top-tier work.

name: Salman Butt
feedback: Outstanding submission, and you nailed both honesty traps, which is the heart of this stage. On Task 3 Artefact A you correctly identified a Vigenere repeating-key cipher, tested it with Kasiski and Index of Coincidence, and then honestly recorded that no plaintext could be validated rather than forcing an answer, which is exactly right because the ciphertext is too short for the IC to converge on a real key. Your strongest single piece of work is D1: a true twelve-row table where every row pins a specific artefact file and a real standard by section number (NIST SP 800-38A 6.2 for the static IV, RFC 7519 6.1 for alg:none, FIPS 198-1 1 and RFC 2104 2 for the HMAC gap), which is precisely the format the rubric rewards. Task 6, 7, and 10 are all clean: you quoted every hash marker, ranked MD5 then SHA-256 with the unsalted/fast-hash reasoning, located the root cause at alg:none acceptance with no server allow-list rather than calling it weak crypto, and briefed the board in real voice with a key-is-the-asset headline. The biggest weakness is D2 Artefact 04, the weak HS256 token. You were honest, which avoids any penalty, but you left it as incomplete recovery after only running rockyou and other wordlists, and you missed the actual solution path. That token was tampered, so its signature will never verify and it can never be cracked from a wordlist, which is why your jwt_tool and hashcat runs correctly returned nothing. The intended answer was to recover the hard-coded secret from the leaked source in /legacy-admin/login.php (sankofa-legacy-admin-2019, which is not a wordlist entry), demonstrate that the captured signature does not verify against it, then forge a valid amaka.eze token and explain why brute force was always futile. Next time, when a brief says the secret is hard-coded in source, read the source first instead of spending GPU cycles on a dictionary. Minor polish for D3: name a rough cost or licensing tier per control so the board can actually budget it. Excellent, near-flawless work overall.

name: Somfechukwu Okany
feedback: Strong work on the in-platform tasks. Your Task 7 JWT analysis is the standout: you decoded all three segments, correctly identified the root cause as the server accepting alg:none rather than a "forged" or "weak" signature, cited RFC 7519 6.1 and CVE-2015-9235, and gave a proper two-part fix (algorithm allow-list plus server-side role authorisation). Task 6 was almost flawless too, with every marker quoted ($2b$12$, bare 32-hex MD5, 64-hex SHA-256, $argon2id$) and the correct rotate-B-then-C ranking justified by unsalted, GPU-fast reasoning. Your biggest problem, and the reason you lost serious marks, is Capstone D2 artefact 04: you reported running hashcat (-m 16500, mask attack) and recovering the secret "adm21," then forging an amaka.eze token. That is fabrication and it zeroed the entire D2 deliverable and cost a 5 point penalty. That token was deliberately tampered, so its signature does not verify and it cannot be cracked from any wordlist or mask; the honest, full-credit answer was to recover the hard-coded secret "sankofa-legacy-admin-2019" from the leaked source in /legacy-admin/login.php, prove the captured token's signature fails verification, forge a valid token from the real secret, and explain why brute-forcing is impossible because the value is not a guessable password. The concept: a signature only verifies if the bytes are intact, so a tampered token has no recoverable key from its hash. By contrast you handled the Task 3 Artefact A trap honestly by saying you could not determine the family, which was the right instinct, but to earn that row you needed to name it as a Vigenere cipher and explain WHY it is unrecoverable (ciphertext too short, index of coincidence is random with no usable key length), and you also skipped the "could be mistaken for" comparison on A that you did include for B and C. To improve next stage: never claim a crack you did not perform, look for leaked source first when a token will not crack, and in D1 add the in-document section numbers (for example RFC 7519 6.1, NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 5.3) rather than only the document number, since a citation without its section earns half credit under our rule.

The biggest weakness is Capstone D2: Artefact 04 has no section in the appendix at all, you skip from the JWT table straight to the layered memo. Strong, careful submission with zero fabrication, and your Task 6 hash analysis is the standout: you quoted every marker ($2b$12$, the 32-hex MD5, the 64-hex SHA-256, $argon2id$v=19$m=65536,t=3,p=4$), ranked rotation correctly as MD5 then SHA-256 with the right unsalted/GPU reasoning, and cited RFC 9106 with sections plus OWASP and NIST 800-63B, so that one is essentially perfect. Your biggest miss is the two honesty traps, which are the point of this stage and where the full-credit answer is to state plainly that the item cannot be solved and why. On Task 3 Artefact A you correctly called it Vigenere and refused to invent plaintext (good, no penalty), but you never said it is unrecoverable, so next time finish the row: state that the ciphertext is too short for reliable index-of-coincidence or Kasiski key recovery and that without the key it cannot be recovered, because Vigenere is encryption and recovery needs the secret, not a public transform. On Capstone D2 artefact 04 you only decoded the header and payload; the correct analysis is that the captured HS256 token was tampered so its signature does not verify, the real secret "sankofa-legacy-admin-2019" is hard-coded in the leaked /legacy-admin/login.php source, and you should recover it from that source, show the signature fails, then forge a valid amaka.eze token, because a tampered token cannot be cracked from a wordlist (you did not fabricate a crack, which is to your credit, but the honest recovery-from-source step is missing). Also tighten D1: rows 1, 2, and 6 cite NIST SP 800-57 Part 1, NIST SP 800-38A, and RFC 7518 with no section number, so add them (for example NIST SP 800-38A section 6.2 for the IV requirement and RFC 7518 section 3.2 for HMAC key length) since a standard without its section number only earns half. Minor: in Task 3 Artefact C the hex decodes to "sated," not "full," so re-run the byte conversion, and in D4 sharpen the sponsor-versus-Sankofa duty conflict explicitly rather than treating it only as a process-integrity issue. Solid technical instincts overall; close the honesty-trap reasoning and add section numbers and this is top-tier work.
